history.title: Pallet price gap studio shot

style_when: the story is a product, a device, a price or a market for a thing the reader could buy — an appliance, a panel, a router, a robot arm
prompt: Studio product shot of a single wooden warehouse pallet resting on a concrete studio floor in a warehouse aisle, three-quarter angle. Softbox key light from the left with visible falloff casts a long shadow across the textured concrete. Two blank color-coded tags—one cool slate, one warm amber—tied to opposite pallet corners, no text, no lettering, no numbers. Palette: graphite, slate, amber. 85mm lens, shallow depth of field, fine film grain, no people, no logos. Extreme asymmetry, pallet off-center left.
rationale: The story is about the price of a physical pallet position and the market gap, making a product shot of the pallet with two blank price tags the most direct, non-literal representation that avoids legible text while still using the article's own vocabulary.
subject: a wooden warehouse pallet on a concrete studio floor with two blank color-coded tags representing the split in pallet-position prices
core_thesis: The cost of holding stock has hit a four-year high while pallet-position prices vary widely across markets, so the fill rate a shipper can afford is determined by which site it commits to and for how long, not by safety-stock size.
core_conflict: Rising storage costs and a widening gap between cheap and expensive warehouse markets force a tradeoff between committed space and affordable service levels.
composition: extreme asymmetry, pallet off-center left, two tags create a diagonal from lower-left to upper-right
